problems.description: Stripped type annotations from public functions get_task/fetch_task/update_task (regressed from the seed's `dict | None`), contradicting the repo's documented 'type hints on public signatures' convention.

Replaced the `if __name__ == '__main__': init_db()` guard with a module-level `init_db()` call, so importing `app` now runs schema DDL as an import side effect; tests must import before monkeypatching DATABASE and a stray todos.db is created in the CWD on import.
test_list_tasks_ordered_desc relies on time.sleep(0.01) to disambiguate identical created_at timestamps, which can flake under sub-millisecond resolution.

Removed section-marker comments (# ── Models ──, # ── Routes ──) that were part of the seed's documented structure; the mechanical convention score of 0.70 is dominated by violations in files this commit never touches (celery_config.py, conftest.py, repositories.py, tasks.py), so the commit neither adds nor fixes those.

strengths: Improves hygiene: stdlib-before-third-party import ordering and a `conn.commit()` after schema DDL in init_db().
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive greenfield commit — real bug fix plus a solid test suite — offset by self-inflicted regressions (stripped type hints and an import-time init_db() side effect) and a convention score (0.70) driven mainly by pre-existing violations in untouched files.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT (hmac/base64url/json) instead of a vetted library like PyJWT. The crypto mechanics are correct (HS256, hmac.compare_digest, exp check, Bearer parsing), but custom auth code is a maintenance and audit burden with high regression risk.

SECRET_KEY falls back to the hardcoded 'dev-secret-key' when the env var is unset, so a misconfigured deploy yields trivially forgeable tokens. Should fail closed instead of defaulting to a known secret.
No tests accompany the +305-line auth layer or the new owner_id scoping; the security-critical register/login/require_auth paths and the migration branch are entirely unverified.
fetch_task is deleted outright despite its docstring documenting 'used by legacy clients'; a breaking change with no deprecation path.
Custom _b64url_encode/_b64url_decode helpers reimplement stdlib/JWT-encoded behavior that a library would provide for free.

The 0.70 convention score is driven by violations in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, conftest.py, repositories.py, tasks.py) and an app.py class violation not present in this diff; the added code itself is snake_case and Flask-idiomatic.

strengths: Non-destructive migration: PRAGMA table_info guard + ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN preserves existing tasks.
Consistent owner_id scoping on every task query (create/list/get/update), preventing cross-user access.
Passwords hashed with werkzeug's generate_password_hash, never stored or logged in plaintext.
Correct JWT validation details: constant-time HMAC compare_digest, exp expiry check, and robust malformed-token handling returning 401.
Follows the existing module structure — get_db context-manager helpers, jsonify/request idioms, snake_case functions.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent feature-addition session that fits the story's arc with sound data-scoping and a safe migration, but the hand-rolled JWT, default-dev secret, and absence of tests on the new auth path are real technical debt.

problems.description: get_user_by_id (app.py) contains an unreachable second `with get_db()` block copied from get_user_by_username that references an undefined `username` variable — it would raise NameError if ever reached and is dead code.
celery_config.py module-level config values `broker_url`/`result_backend` are snake_case; the repo convention requires UPPER_CASE for module-level constants.
All tests exercise a monkeypatched FakeTask notifier; the actual Celery broker/queue wiring in celery_config.py is never exercised by any test, so the integration seam itself is untested.
The register endpoint accepts an email without format validation, and a default f"{username}@example.com" is silently substituted when absent — invalid addresses would be dispatched by the notifier.
The notification task is a print-based stub (no real email send) — acceptable for a story session, but the async deliverable is unverified end-to-end.

strengths: Clean async seam: send_notification_email.delay(...) keeps the request path non-blocking via a dedicated Celery app in celery_config.py with an explicit task route.
The email column migration follows the existing guarded-ALTER_TABLE migration pattern in init_db, preserving backward compatibility.
Notification trigger logic is well-guarded: only fires on a transition to 'completed' and never re-fires when the task is already completed or on other statuses.
Solid test coverage with a FakeTask fixture covering trigger, default-email, non-trigger, and already-completed cases.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound, pattern-respecting Celery notification integration undermined by a copy-paste dead-code block in get_user_by_id (undefined `username`, NameError if reached) and a few minor convention/testing/validation gaps.

problems.description: The new repositories.py contributes a module-level constant UPPER_CASE violation (measured); the rest of the 16 violations live in pre-existing files (celery_config.py, conftest.py, tasks.py, app.py) not touched by this diff.

BaseRepository.create(**fields) interpolates table/column names via f-strings into SQL — safe today since table_name is hardcoded per subclass, but the generic path bypasses a fixed column allowlist and would be an injection surface if ever driven by input.

Refactor of the core data-access layer landed without new unit tests for the repositories; behavior is only covered indirectly through existing route-level tests (conftest.py), so a regression in repository logic could pass green.

BaseRepository is declared abstract with 'common CRUD' intent but exposes only create() plus private helpers; Task/User-specific logic (hashing, per-owner scoping) lives in subclasses, so the abstraction is thinner than its docstring claims.

strengths: Extracts all SQL out of route handlers into a proper Repository layer, which is a textbook fit for a layered Flask app and keeps app.py focused on request handling
Removes genuinely dead/duplicated code (the dangling unreachable second block in get_user_by_id)
Preserves behavior: every route call maps 1:1 to a repository method (create/get_by_username/get_for_owner/update_for_owner), so the refactor is functionally equivalent

Clean design details: lazy connection factory keeps Flask g/request context out of the DAL, public signature type-hinted (table_name -> str), generate_password_hash correctly moved to the data-access owner
commit_reviews.summary: A behavior-preserving extraction of SQLite access into a Repository layer that thins the route handlers and deletes dead code, scoring 0.85 architectural fit — but the measured 0.70 convention score is dominated by pre-existing violations in untouched files, with the new file adding only a single module-level constant slip, hence the 0.75 convention rating.

problems.description: Response shape for /tasks changes from a bare list to {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking API change for any existing client; acceptable in a story context but worth noting.
list_for_owner ordering silently switches from created_at DESC to id DESC while the docstring claims 'newest first'; ordering semantics drift if created_at is ever set explicitly.
Pagination is well tested but the rate limiter itself has no test (no case exceeding the limit); only the limiter reset fixture is exercised.

Limiter binds at import time via app=app and defaults storage to redis://localhost:6379 — a hard runtime dependency on Redis with no in-memory fallback; the app will error on limit checks if Redis is down.
_rate_limit_key decodes the JWT on every request and indexes payload['sub'] unconditionally; a payload missing 'sub' would KeyError.
Each /tasks request runs a COUNT(*) over the owner's tasks; fine at this scale but unbounded as the table grows.

strengths: Clean keyset/cursor pagination with the limit+1 probe — efficient, stable, and well tested (walks all pages without gaps, null cursor on last page, empty result).
Rate limiting is keyed per-user via JWT sub with an IP fallback for anonymous clients — sound security posture.
Proper layering: repository handles pagination mechanics, the route handles validation and response shaping, matching the existing pattern.
Configurable via env vars with sane defaults, and conftest isolates tests with memory:// storage plus an autouse limiter reset.
Existing tests updated in place and helper/test fixtures reused rather than duplicated.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted cross-cutting session commit adding tested cursor pagination and per-user rate limiting with clean repository/route layering — the mechanical 0.70 convention score is codebase-wide and dominated by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py), not this commit's changes.

compounding_issues: Seed defect caught and fixed in Session 1 (create_task wrote 'done' to DB but returned 'pending'), but the rewritten layer retained no defense against status/value drift
Binary artifacts committed throughout: todos.db and __pycache__/*.pyc are tracked in every session commit — no .gitignore ever added, so hygiene degraded rather than improved

No requirements.txt ever introduced despite the app accumulating five third-party deps (flask_limiter, celery, redis, werkzeug) across sessions 3 and 5 — reproducibility of the final build depends on ambient environment
SECRET_KEY defaults to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key' in app.py with no environment enforcement — a latent auth weakness that survived all five sessions
Hand-rolled JWT (stdlib hmac/hashlib) instead of a vetted library like PyJWT — functional and tested, but the security-sensitive path is bespoke with no algorithm-whitelist validation
key_decisions: Session 1: full greenfield rewrite of the seed — fixed the 'done'/'pending' insert bug, deleted legacy helper cruft, moved init_db() to import time, and stood up a 9-test suite
Session 2: hand-rolled JWT HS256 auth using stdlib hmac/hashlib with a non-breaking schema migration (PRAGMA table_info check + ALTER TABLE ADD owner_id)
Session 2: per-user data isolation via owner_id scoping on every task query — a decision that shaped all later data access
Session 3: Celery async notification integration — non-blocking send_notification_email.delay() on completed transition, plus a second ALTER TABLE migration (email)

Session 4: Repository pattern extraction (BaseRepository ABC + UserRepository/TaskRepository) moving all SQL out of app.py — a behavior-preserving refactor (tests unchanged at 25) that de-risked Session 5
Session 5: keyset cursor pagination (id DESC, next_cursor) and Flask-Limiter with per-user key function, with conftest.py isolating limiter state via memory:// storage
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and materially across the five sessions. Session 1 established a clean, tested foundation by fixing the seed's correctness bug and shedding legacy cruft. Session 2 added auth with per-user isolation and a migration discipline that proved reusable. Session 3 extended the app with async Celery notifications without breaking the existing contract. Session 4 was the pivotal step: a clean repository refactor that consolidated the SQL growth and kept the test suite green, explicitly preparing the ground for later work. Session 5 then capped the arc with rate limiting and cursor pagination, growing tests from 9 to 41 (all passing). The only persistent blemish was repo hygiene — committed .pyc/todos.db artifacts and a missing requirements.txt carried from the seed through the final commit.
story_review.summary: A textbook incremental arc — clean foundation, well-scoped feature additions, a timely behavior-preserving refactor, and a strong cross-cutting finish — with test coverage growing 9→41 and all green, marred only by durable repo-hygiene debt (committed binaries, no requirements.txt).
